33952: He paints the terrors that pursue the wicked, then in a very short last speech says that if even the moon and stars are not pure before God, a mortal "maggot" cannot be.
33953: Bildad is the second of Job's three friends. He defends God's justice by appealing to tradition and the wisdom of the fathers, and bluntly suggests that Job's children died because they sinned. His speeches grow shorter as the debate goes on; his last is only six verses long.
33954: Shuah is the name of a son of Abraham and Keturah (Gen 25:2), so "Shuhite" may point to an Arabian or Aramean tribe (speculative). God's rebuke includes him (Job 42:9).
33955: Blunt and conservative, quoting the ancestors and short on sympathy.
33958: God exacts less than you deserve
33959: He tells Job that if God spoke, Job would learn that God is punishing him less than his guilt deserves, and that God's wisdom is beyond searching out.
33960: The triumph of the wicked is short
33961: Feeling insulted, he describes how the wicked man's prosperity vanishes like a dream and how God's anger rains down on him.
33962: Zophar is the third and most abrasive of Job's friends. He tells Job outright that he deserves worse than he is getting, and he describes the swift ruin of the wicked. He speaks only twice; in the third round of speeches he is silent, or his speech may have been displaced (debated).
33963: His home, Naamah, is unknown; a town of that name in Judah (Josh 15:41) is probably not meant. God's rebuke includes him (Job 42:9).
33965: Many scholars think the third cycle of speeches (Job 24-27) has been disturbed in transmission and that parts of Job 27 originally belonged to Zophar; others read his silence as deliberate, showing the friends have run out of arguments. This is debated.
33966: Hot-tempered and dogmatic, impatient with talk and quick to assume the worst.
33970: Buz (perhaps an Aramean or Arabian people)
33971: Young speaker in the book of Job
33973: A younger man who had waited out of respect, he grew angry at Job for justifying himself rather than God, and at the friends for condemning Job without an answer. He says it is the Spirit in a person, not age, that gives understanding.
33974: Suffering as God's warning and teaching
33975: He argues that God speaks through dreams and through pain to turn people from pride and to save their lives, and that God delivers the afflicted by their affliction.
33976: Points to God in the storm
33977: He ends by describing God's majesty in thunder, snow and lightning, preparing the way for God's own speech from the whirlwind.
33978: Elihu is a young man who suddenly speaks for six chapters after Job and his three friends fall silent. He rejects both Job's self-defence and the friends' accusations, and argues that God uses suffering to teach and warn, not only to punish. God neither praises nor rebukes him at the end, which has left readers divided over whether he is wise, presumptuous, or both.
33979: He is the son of Barachel the Buzite, of the family of Ram (Job 32:2). Buz is named as a nephew of Abraham (Gen 22:21). He is not introduced in the prologue or mentioned in the epilogue.
33980: Many scholars think the Elihu speeches were added to the book later, because he is absent from the frame story, his style differs, and he partly anticipates God's speeches (debated).
33982: Some Christian interpreters, and Jewish commentators such as Maimonides in part, see Elihu as closer to the truth than the friends: suffering can refine and instruct, and he prepares for God's appearance. God's silence about him is read as approval.
33984: Others see a long-winded young man who claims to bring something new but largely repeats the friends; his wordiness may be gently mocked by the text.
33985: Earnest, eager and wordy, apologising for speaking up and then speaking at great length, with flashes of real insight about God in the storm.
33991: He confesses he has not learned wisdom or the knowledge of the Holy One, asks who has gone up to heaven and come down, affirms that every word of God is tested, prays for neither poverty nor riches, and gathers numerical sayings ("three things... yes, four").
33992: Agur son of Jakeh is the author of Proverbs 30, known only from that chapter. His sayings begin with a humble confession of ignorance before God, include a famous prayer for "neither poverty nor riches", and collect observations about nature and human behaviour in numbered lists.
33993: His words are called a massa, which can mean "oracle" or refer to Massa, a tribe descended from Ishmael (Gen 25:14). The questions "what is his name, and what is his son's name?" (Prov 30:4) are often discussed.
33994: Some rabbinic tradition reads "Agur son of Jakeh" as a symbolic name for Solomon (tradition).
33995: Most scholars treat Agur as a non-Israelite sage, perhaps from Massa, whose wisdom was included in Israel's collection (scholarly-consensus that he is distinct from Solomon; his origin is debated).
33996: Many Christian readers hear in Prov 30:4 a hint of a divine Son, while others take it as a rhetorical question stressing that no human can know God fully.
33997: Humble, wry and searching, a sage who begins by admitting how little he knows and then notices everything.
34002: His mother warned him not to give his strength to women or kings' ruin to wine, and charged him to "open your mouth for the mute" and defend the rights of the poor and needy.
34003: Lemuel is an unknown king whose mother's advice is recorded in Proverbs 31:1-9. She warns him against sexual excess and drink, and calls him to speak up for those who cannot speak for themselves. The poem on the capable wife that follows (Prov 31:10-31) may or may not be part of her teaching.
34004: The words are "the oracle (or: of Massa) which his mother taught him" (Prov 31:1). It is the only teaching in Proverbs explicitly credited to a woman.
34006: Lemuel is often taken as a name for Solomon, and the teacher as Bathsheba (tradition).
34007: Most scholars see Lemuel as a non-Israelite king, perhaps of Massa, like Agur (debated). Whether the acrostic poem on the woman of strength belongs to his mother's words is also debated.
34008: Respectful and attentive, a king who repeats his mother's words as she spoke them, with a ruler's concern for justice.
34010: Sounds like the Hebrew for "pain" (a wordplay explained in the text)
34013: His mother named him because she bore him in pain. He called on the God of Israel to bless him, enlarge his territory, keep God's hand with him, and keep him from harm so that it would not pain him. God granted his request.
34014: Jabez appears in just two verses in the genealogy of Judah. He was "more honourable than his brothers", and his name, which sounds like "pain", recalled his difficult birth. He prayed that God would bless him, widen his land and keep him from harm, and God answered. His era is not stated; the setting suggests the time of the settlement in Canaan (speculative).
34015: The Chronicler pauses a list of names to tell this short story (1 Chr 4:9-10). A town called Jabez, home to scribal families, is mentioned earlier (1 Chr 2:55); the link is uncertain.
34017: Bruce Wilkinson's *The Prayer of Jabez* (2000) encouraged believers to pray this prayer daily for expanded blessing and influence; it sold millions of copies.
34019: Many scholars and pastors caution that the passage describes one man's prayer and God's answer, not a formula, and that it should be read alongside Scripture's wider teaching on suffering and contentment.
34020: Rabbinic tradition identifies Jabez with Othniel the judge and reads his prayer as a request for Torah learning (tradition, Babylonian Talmud Temurah 16a).
34021: Earnest and direct, the voice of someone who has carried a hard name all his life and asks God plainly for a better story.
